claim: The Hispanic Community Health Study/Study of Latinos (HCHS/SOL) is the largest genetic study of Hispanics/Latinos in the U.S. to date.
source: In this study, we utilize the largest genetic study of Hispanics/Latinos in the U.S. to date -- the Hispanic Community Health Study/Study of Latinos (HCHS/SOL) (Conomos et al., 2016)
evidence: The manuscript directly states this is the largest genetic study of Hispanics/Latinos in the U.S. to date, with citation to Conomos et al., 2016

claim: Amerindigenous ancestry increased by an average of ~20% spanning 1940s-1990s in Mexican Americans.
source: Using genotype data from the Hispanic Community Health Study/Study of Latinos, we find that Amerindigenous ancestry increased by an average of ~20% spanning 1940s-1990s in Mexican Americans.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by data shown in Figure 2 and Table 1

claim: Polygenic risk scores based on summary statistics from a European-based genome-wide association study perform poorly in Mexican Americans for height.
source: We show for height how polygenic risk scores based on summary statistics from a European-based genome-wide association study perform poorly in Mexican Americans.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by analysis shown in Figure 4C and Supplementary file 5

claim: The United States Census Bureau defines Hispanic/Latino ethnicity as a category for individuals who self-identify as 'a person of Cuban, Mexican, Puerto Rican, South or Central American, or other Spanish culture or origin regardless of race'.
source: The United States Census Bureau refers to the Hispanic/Latino ethnicity as a category for individuals who self-identify as 'a person of Cuban, Mexican, Puerto Rican, South or Central American, or other Spanish culture or origin regardless of race (United States Government, Executive Office of the President, Office of Management and Budget, Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs, 1997).
evidence: This is a direct citation to a government document defining the Hispanic/Latino category

claim: Individuals who identify as Hispanic/Latino have varying proportions of Amerindigenous, African, and European genetic ancestries.
source: Individuals who identify as Hispanic/Latino have varying proportions of Amerindigenous, African, and European genetic ancestries, each with their own unique continental demographic history.
evidence: This is supported by the ternary plots in Figure 1A-B showing the distribution of three-way ancestry proportions

claim: Demographic forces such as population bottlenecks, expansions, and migration as well as adaptation to novel environments resulted in observable differences in continental patterns of genetic variation.
source: Demographic forces such as population bottlenecks, expansions, and migration as well as adaptation to novel environments resulted in observable differences in continental patterns of genetic variation (Nelson et al., 2008; Abecasis et al., 2012; Auton et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research

claim: The founding of the Americas by Amerindigenous populations, the colonization by Europeans, and the African slave trade shaped genetic diversity in Hispanic/Latino populations.
source: These differing patterns were shaped by many historical events of migration which included the founding of the Americas by Amerindigenous populations, the colonization by Europeans, and the African slave trade (Gravel et al., 2013; Homburger et al., 2015; Moreno-Estrada et al., 2014; Moreno-Estrada et al., 2013; Reich et al., 2012; Bryc et al., 2015; Conomos et al., 2016; Han et al., 2017; Baharian et al., 2016; Jordan et al., 2019; Micheletti et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research on admixture history

claim: Demographic history has shaped the genetic architecture of modern human phenotypic variation.
source: Demographic history has shaped the genetic architecture of modern human phenotypic variation (Agarwala et al., 2013; Eyre-Walker, 2010; Maher et al., 2013; Simons et al., 2014; Uricchio et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research

claim: By 2044 the United States is predicted to become a 'minority-majority' country whereby no one racial/ethnic group comprises more than 50% of the population.
source: The demography of the United States has changed drastically over the 20th century, and by 2044 is predicted to become a 'minority-majority' country whereby no one racial/ethnic group comprises more than 50% of the population.
evidence: This is a demographic projection about future US population composition

claim: By 2060 Hispanics/Latinos are projected to make up 29% of the US population or 119 million individuals.
source: By 2060 Hispanics/Latinos are projected to make up 29% of the US population or 119 million individuals (Colby and Ortman, 2015).
evidence: This is a demographic projection cited from Colby and Ortman, 2015

claim: Population-based medical genomics research has been disproportionately focused on individuals of European descent.
source: However, to date, population-based medical genomics research [and its subsequent benefits, including polygenic risk score (PRS) profiling] have been disproportionately focused on individuals of European descent, with the findings primarily benefiting European populations (Bustamante et al., 2011; Martin et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research on diversity in genomics studies

claim: Hispanic or Latin American participation in genome-wide association studies (GWAS) has continued to hover around 1%.
source: Despite the increases in sample sizes, rates of discovery, and traits studied, Hispanic or Latin American participation in genome-wide association studies (GWAS) has continued to hover around 1% (Popejoy and Fullerton, 2016; Mills and Rahal, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research on GWAS diversity

claim: 10,268 unrelated HCHS/SOL individuals were analyzed for global ancestry estimates.
source: Using the subset of sites that overlapped with our African, European, and Amerindigenous reference panels, we called 3-way global ancestry estimates for 10,268 unrelated HCHS/SOL individuals (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the sample size used in the analysis

claim: Dominicans have the highest average proportions of African ancestry among HCHS/SOL populations.
source: We find that Dominicans, who have the highest average proportions of African ancestry, are in the middle, with Puerto Ricans and Cubans, diverging in opposite directions (Figure 1D) with clines of increasing European ancestry proportions (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1C-D showing ancestry proportions

claim: Mexican Americans and Central/South American groups form large, separate wings that diverge from Cubans and Dominicans in UMAP analysis.
source: Further, while self-identified Mexican, Central, and South American groups appear to have overlapping ancestry proportions in Figure 1A–B, UMAP represents the Mexican Americans and Central/South American groups as large, separate wings that diverge from self-identified Cubans and Dominicans, with both clusters diverging with clines of increasing ancestry toward different Amerindigenous (AI) populations (Figure 1C–D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by UMAP visualizations in Figure 1C-D

claim: The increase in AI global ancestry over time in Mexican Americans was consistent across multiple data stratifications including recruitment region, US-born or not US-born, educational attainment, and gender.
source: In Mexican Americans, the increase in AI global ancestry over time was consistent across multiple data stratifications including recruitment region, US-born or not US-born, educational attainment, and gender (Table 1 and Supplementary file 2)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Table 1

claim: There are significant differences in AI ancestry between recruitment regions in Mexican Americans.
source: We identified significant differences in AI ancestry between recruitment region (t-test, 95% CI:0.12–0.15, p<2.2E-16)
evidence: This is stated with specific statistical test results

claim: There are significant differences in AI ancestry between US-born and not US-born Mexican Americans.
source: US-born or not US-born individuals (t-test, 95% CI:0.06–0.09, p<2.2E-16)
evidence: This is stated with specific statistical test results

claim: Educational attainment is significantly associated with AI ancestry in Mexican Americans.
source: and educational attainment, which can be considered a proxy for socioeconomic status (one-way ANOVA, p<2E-16).
evidence: This is stated with specific statistical test results

claim: On average, global AI ancestry has increased ~20% over the 50 year period for Mexican Americans born from 1940 to 1990.
source: On average, global AI ancestry has increased ~20% over the 50 year period for Mexican Americans born from 1940 to 1990.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2B showing bootstrap resampling results

claim: The increase in global AI ancestry over time was replicated in an independent cohort of self-identified Mexican Americans from the Health and Retirement Study (HRS).
source: We replicated the increase in global AI ancestry over time in a smaller, independent cohort of self-identified Mexican Americans (n = 705) from the Health and Retirement Study (HRS) (Fisher and Ryan, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific sample size and citation

claim: HRS Mexican Americans have lower levels of global AI ancestry on average (mean = 0.29) compared to HCHS/SOL Mexican Americans.
source: The HRS Mexican Americans are older compared to the HCHS/SOL Mexican Americans (birth year distribution: 1915–1981; mean = 1943, median:1942) and have lower levels of global AI ancestry on average (mean = 0.29)
evidence: This is a direct comparison of ancestry levels between two cohorts

claim: For US-born Mexican Americans with both parents born outside the US, there is a strong positive relationship between birth year and increase in AI ancestry (β=0.004; 95% CI: 0.0034-0.0046; p=4.85e-12).
source: We found a strong positive relationship between estimated birth year and increase in AI ancestry for those with both parents born outside the US, who formed the baseline group in this model (β=0.004; 95% CI: 0.0034-0.0046; p=4.85e-12) (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is stated with specific effect size and statistical significance

claim: FST estimates within AI ancestry tracts between birth-decades are negligible with many estimates below 0.
source: Figure 3—figure supplement 1 shows all pairwise comparisons among birth-decades, and demonstrates that while the estimates of FST are negligible (with many estimates below 0), there is a subtle trend of increasing FST as birth-decade differences increase (though individuals born in the 80 s and 90 s show a conflicting pattern).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: No loci were significantly associated with birth year across the genome in admixture mapping analysis.
source: Although we tried two different models (see Materials and methods), we did not find any loci to be significantly associated with birth year across the genome (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: There is a significant positive correlation between birth year and total ROH in Mexican Americans (τ = 0.0449, p=6.12e-5).
source: Overall, we find a significant positive correlation between birth year and the total ROH (summed across size classes; τ = 0.0449, p=6.12e-5, Kendall's rank correlation)
evidence: This is stated with specific correlation coefficient and p-value

claim: The correlation between birth year and ROH becomes stronger when restricted to ROH calls that overlap AI ancestry tracts (τ=0.065, p=7.39e-9).
source: but this signal becomes stronger when we restrict our analysis to ROH calls that overlap AI ancestry tracts (τ=0.065, p=7.39e-9).
evidence: This is stated with specific correlation coefficient and p-value

claim: The associations in AI ROH with birth year are primarily driven by short (τ=0.097, p<2.2E-16) and medium (τ=0.084, p=1.27E-13) size classes.
source: When stratified by size class and normalized by AI global ancestry, the associations (all Kendall's rank correlation) in AI ROH were primarily driven by the short (τ=0.097, p<2.2E-16), and medium (τ=0.084, p=1.27E-13) size classes
evidence: This is stated with specific correlation coefficients and p-values

claim: There is a significant negative correlation between birth year and total ROH that overlap European ancestry tracts (τ=−0.089, p=1.82E-14).
source: We observed the opposite pattern when ROH were restricted to European ancestry segments of the genome: there is a significant negative correlation between birth year and the total ROH that overlap European ancestry tracts (τ=−0.089, p=1.82E-14).
evidence: This is stated with specific correlation coefficient and p-value

claim: Inferred biological parental AI ancestries are significantly correlated in HCHS/SOL Mexican Americans (r = 0.708, 95% CI:0.69–0.72, p<2.2E-16).
source: With individuals from all decades pooled together, we found the inferred biological parental AI ancestries to be significantly correlated (Figure 3D, r = 0.708, 95% CI:0.69–0.72, p<2.2E-16, Pearson correlation).
evidence: This is stated with specific correlation coefficient and p-value, and supported by Figure 3D

claim: The correlation in inferred parental AI global ancestry ranged from 0.65 to 0.74 when stratified by decade.
source: When stratified by decade, the distributions of the difference in parental AI overlap each other and the correlation in inferred parental AI global ancestry ranged from 0.65 to 0.74 (Figure 3—figure supplement 4)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 4

claim: Population growth does not cause systematic changes in the frequency of segregating neutral alleles.
source: While population growth can intensify the strength of natural selection (causing deleterious alleles to decrease in frequency and adaptive alleles to increase in frequency), population growth does not cause systematic changes in the frequency of segregating neutral alleles.
evidence: This is a statement about population genetic theory

claim: Including population growth in simulations did not affect the mean ancestry proportion in a population.
source: Similarly, including population growth did not affect the mean ancestry proportion in a population (Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by simulation results in Figure 3—figure supplement 6

claim: Ancestry-based assortative mating does not induce changes in mean ancestry proportions in the population.
source: Ancestry-based assortative mating can lead to increased ROH and decreased genetic diversity (see Figure 3), but because mating occurs from individuals proportionally across the ancestry spectrum, ancestry-based assortative mating does not induce any changes in mean ancestry proportions in the population (albeit with slight increase in variance in ancestry proportions over time, Figure 3—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by simulation results in Figure 3—figure supplement 7

claim: Ancestry-based fecundity differences can induce systematic changes in ancestry proportions in the population.
source: Ancestry-based fecundity differences can induce systematic changes in ancestry proportions in the population (Figure 3—figure supplement 8B–E)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by simulation results in Figure 3—figure supplement 8

claim: Ancestry-based assortative mating can magnify the effects of ancestry-based fecundity differences.
source: Further, ancestry-based assortative mating can magnify the effects of ancestry-based fecundity differences (Figure 3—figure supplement 8F–I).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by simulation results in Figure 3—figure supplement 8

claim: 18 of 69 biomedical traits (26%) are significantly associated with AI ancestry in Mexican Americans after adjusting for multiple factors.
source: As illustrated in Figure 4A, 18 of these traits (26%) are significantly associated with AI ancestry (Bonferroni correction p<6.6E-5) after adjusting for several factors including birth year, center, gender, sampling weight, educational attainment, US-born status, and number of US-born parents.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4A

claim: Height has the strongest association with global AI ancestry among the traits tested.
source: Among the traits we tested for association with global AI ancestry, height had the strongest effect.
evidence: This is stated in the text and can be seen in Figure 4A

claim: All quartiles of global AI ancestry have increased in height by a similar amount over the period investigated.
source: Indeed, when we stratified individuals by quartiles of global AI ancestry, we see that all quartiles have increased in height by a similar amount over the period investigated (though individuals with lower AI ancestry were taller on average).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4B

claim: There was no significant effect of birth year on polygenic height score (p=0.14).
source: However, we did not find a significant effect of birth year on PHS (Figure 4—figure supplement 3; p=0.14)
evidence: This is stated with specific p-value and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 3

claim: Migration from Mexico to the US has shifted over the years from states with less Amerindigenous ancestry to states with higher Amerindigenous ancestry.
source: Independent analyses have shown that migration from Mexico to the US has shifted over the years from states with less Amerindigenous ancestry to states with higher Amerindigenous ancestry (Moreno-Estrada et al., 2014; Terrazas, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research

claim: Hispanic/Latino is the fastest growing ethnicity in the US according to census data.
source: Third, from US census data, we know that Hispanic/Latino is the fastest growing ethnicity (with Mexican Americans constituting the plurality).
evidence: This is stated as knowledge from US census data

claim: Individuals with lower percentages of AI ancestry were taller on average than individuals with higher AI ancestry.
source: Individuals with lower percentages of AI ancestry were taller on average than individuals with higher AI ancestry pointing to the role of AI ancestry on the trait.
evidence: This is stated in the text and can be seen in Figure 4B

claim: PRS are most effective in populations of European descent as GWAS studies have been primarily performed in these populations.
source: PRS are most effective in populations of European descent as GWAS studies have been primarily performed in these populations (Bustamante et al., 2011; Martin et al., 2019; Popejoy and Fullerton, 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research

claim: PRS are expected to be biased when applied to non-European populations due to differences in the genetic architecture of traits across diverse populations.
source: and are expected to be biased when applied to other populations due to differences in the genetic architecture of traits across diverse populations (Martin et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research

claim: Allele frequencies for height-associated SNPs between the 1000 Genomes Americas Superpopulation and UKBB showed good concordance (r = 0.93, 95% CI:0.92–0.94, p<2.2E-16).
source: Allele frequencies for these SNPs between the 1000 Genomes Americas Superpopulation and UKBB showed good concordance (Figure 4—figure supplement 2, r = 0.93, 95% CI:0.92–0.94, p<2.2E-16, Pearson correlation).
evidence: This is stated with specific correlation coefficient and p-value, and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: Mexico's society was largely defined by an established social caste system based on ancestry, which disappeared after Mexico's independence in 1821.
source: Mexico's society was largely defined by an established social caste system based on ancestry, which disappeared after Mexico's independence in 1821 (Lisker et al., 1990).
evidence: This is a historical claim supported by citation

claim: Social inequalities persist in Mexico today with skin color having a significant effect on wealth and education.
source: Even so, social inequalities persist today with skin color having a significant effect on wealth and education (Martinez, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research

claim: Studies using modern Artificial Intelligence techniques have been shown to inflate existing disparities between Black Americans and White Americans.
source: For example, studies that use modern Artificial Intelligence techniques have already been shown to inflate existing disparities between Black Americans and White Americans (Obermeyer et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research

claim: The HCHS/SOL cohort is not representative of all US Hispanics/Latinos.
source: While we have shown a dramatic shift in ancestry proportions in US Hispanic/Latinos, one of the caveats of this study is that the HCHS/SOL cohort is not representative of all US Hispanics/Latinos.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors

claim: HCHS/SOL participants were recruited at four primary centers: Bronx, Chicago, Miami, and San Diego.
source: HCHS/SOL participants were recruited at four primary centers: Bronx, Chicago, Miami, and San Diego.
evidence: This is a description of the study design

claim: 12,434 HCHS/SOL participants with birth year estimates between 1934–1993 consented to genetics studies.
source: 12,434 participants with birth year estimates between 1934–1993 who self-identified as being of Cuban, Dominican, Puerto Rican, Mexican, Central American, or South American background consented to genetics studies and posting of their genetic and phenotype data on the publicly available Database of Genotypes and Phenotypes (dbGaP) through Study Accession phs000810.v1.p1.
evidence: This is a description of the study sample

claim: HCHS/SOL samples were genotyped on an Illumina custom array, SoL HCHS Custom 15041502 array.
source: Samples were genotyped on an Illumina custom array, SoL HCHS Custom 15041502 array (annotation B3, genome build 37), consisting of the Illumina Omni 2.5M array and 148,353 custom single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) (Conomos et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a description of the genotyping platform used

claim: After quality control filtering, 1,763,935 genotyped SNPs with minor allele frequency (MAF) >0.01 remained.
source: Our filtering resulted in 1,763,935 genotyped SNPs with minor allele frequency (MAF) >0.01.
evidence: This is a description of the data after quality control

claim: The reference panel for ancestry inference was comprised of 315 individuals: 104 HapMap phase 3 CEU (European), 107 YRI (African), and 112 Amerindigenous individuals.
source: Ancestral tracts, known as 'local' ancestry, along the genome for all HCHS/SOL individuals were inferred using RFMix (Maples et al., 2013) and a three population reference panel, comprised of 315 individuals: 104 HapMap phase 3 CEU (European) and 107 YRI (African) individuals (Altshuler et al., 2010) and 112 Amerindigenous individuals from throughout Latin America (Reich et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a description of the reference panel composition

claim: The reference panel was limited to individuals with 99% continental ancestry as inferred by unsupervised ADMIXTURE.
source: The reference panel was limited to individuals with 99% continental ancestry as inferred by unsupervised ADMIXTURE (Alexander et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a description of the reference panel quality control

claim: Previous estimates of the generation time in humans resulted in an estimate of ~26–30 years per generation.
source: Previous estimates of the generation time in humans has resulted in an estimate of ~26–30 years per generation (Moorjani et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research

claim: Polygenic risk scores for height were calculated using 1,078 SNPs from UK Biobank GWAS Round 2 Summary Statistics.
source: Risk scores were calculated by extracting the overlapping genome-wide significant hits initially discovered in the UKBB GWASs of height and selecting SNPs with the lowest p-value in each 1 Mb window across the genome. Prior to extraction there were a total of 227,794 genome-wide significant SNPs initially discovered in the UKBB GWAS of height. For height this resulted in a dataset of 1078 overlapping SNPs for the PRS calculation that were present in our dataset of genotyped and imputed SNPs.
evidence: This is a description of the PRS calculation method

claim: The UK Biobank GWAS of height had complete phenotype information for 360,388 individuals.
source: For height, there was complete phenotype information for 360,388 individuals.
evidence: This is information about the UKBB GWAS sample size
